title: Infrastructure pillars
prompt_markdown: Which set contains the three infrastructure pillars introduced in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Deployment, tests, and monitoring

options.label: B
options.text: Compute, storage, and networking

options.label: C
options.text: Development, test, and production

options.label: D
options.text: Applications, users, and code

grader_markdown: Compute executes workloads, storage retains data, and networking connects resources. The alternatives describe activities, environments, or application-level concerns rather than the three infrastructure pillars.

title: Declarative configuration
prompt_markdown: Which statement best describes a declarative infrastructure definition?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a script listing commands to run, in the order an administrator would type them.

options.label: B
options.text: It specifies the exact sequence of operations needed for each possible starting state.

options.label: C
options.text: It describes the desired state, and the tool works out the steps needed to reach it.

options.label: D
options.text: It lets the tool run independent changes in parallel, which is what makes it declarative.

grader_markdown: A declarative definition expresses the intended state. Automation determines the operations needed from the declaration and actual state. Parallel execution may be possible, but it is not what makes a definition declarative, and declarations still have dependencies.

title: Idempotence
prompt_markdown: An automation run has successfully reached the desired state. Its inputs and the relevant external state then remain unchanged. What should a second idempotent run do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the current state, find nothing to change, and make no changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Recreate the resources so the team can show they are still reproducible from the code.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip checking the current state, since the previous run already succeeded, and report success.

options.label: D
options.text: Add another copy of each declared resource.

grader_markdown: Once the desired state is satisfied, repeating an idempotent operation under unchanged relevant conditions should cause no further managed-state changes. Checking the current state is compatible with idempotence; doing nothing without checking does not establish correctness.

title: Cloud service models
prompt_markdown: A team moves from managing virtual machines under IaaS to a managed application platform under PaaS. Which responsibility would typically move towards the provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Deciding which business requirements the application should meet

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining and reviewing the team's own application source code

options.label: C
options.text: Choosing which application features to release and when

options.label: D
options.text: Patching and upgrading the operating system and the runtime

grader_markdown: PaaS typically transfers more operating-system and runtime-platform maintenance to the provider. The exact boundary depends on the service. The application team still owns its business requirements and application code.

title: Version-controlled infrastructure definitions
prompt_markdown: Which pair of benefits best explains how version-controlling infrastructure definitions helps a team deliver changes reliably?

options.label: A
options.text: It preserves change history, so reverting a definition also restores any deleted application data.

options.label: B
options.text: It gives one shared definition, and storing it in Git keeps the running infrastructure in sync with it.

options.label: C
options.text: Changes can be reviewed and checked before they apply, and the history shows who changed what and why.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes environment differences visible, so validation is no longer needed once a change is approved.

grader_markdown: Review and automated checks before application can catch mistakes, as in the lecture's example of firewall rules codified in Git and checked by pipeline policies before they reached the devices. The commit history records who changed what, when, and why, and makes rollback possible. Version control alone neither applies changes nor restores deleted data: in the lecture's rule, code lives in Git and only automation delivers the change. Reviewed changes still need validation.

title: Configuration drift
prompt_markdown: Two servers were created from the same definition. An administrator changes a managed setting manually on one server. Which description and response best address the situation?

options.label: A
options.text: The server has drifted; compare it with the definition, then restore the setting or review and update the definition.

options.label: B
options.text: The definition is now obsolete; copy the new setting into it and apply it to the other server straight away, without a review.

options.label: C
options.text: The servers are still consistent because they came from the same definition, so a note about the manual change in the operations log is enough.

options.label: D
options.text: The difference is a fault in the server; rebuild both servers immediately.

grader_markdown: Drift is a difference between actual managed state and intended state. Investigate it before reconciliation: an unauthorized change may need reversal, while a legitimate change should be reviewed and recorded in the definition. A shared origin does not guarantee continued consistency.

title: Mutable and immutable infrastructure
prompt_markdown: A server needs an operating-system configuration change and stores application data that must survive the update. Which plan correctly distinguishes mutable and immutable approaches?

options.label: A
options.text: A mutable update replaces the server; an immutable update modifies the existing server and keeps its identity and data in place.

options.label: B
options.text: Both approaches modify the existing server; the immutable one also records the change in version control.

options.label: C
options.text: A mutable update changes the existing server; an immutable update replaces it and rebuilds the application data from the infrastructure definition.

options.label: D
options.text: A mutable update changes the existing server; an immutable update replaces it and keeps the data in separate storage or migrates it.

grader_markdown: Mutable updates change an existing instance. Immutable updates replace it with an instance prepared from the updated definition or image. Persistent application data needs separate storage or a verified transfer/recovery process; infrastructure definitions do not generally contain that data.

title: Separating infrastructure and server configuration
prompt_markdown: A deployment needs networks and virtual machines, plus software and service configuration inside those machines. Which organization best separates responsibilities while keeping the deployment coordinated?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep a complete, independent copy of the whole setup for each environment, so that a change made for one environment stays out of the others.

options.label: B
options.text: Separate provisioning from server configuration, pass the needed resource details between them, and review each part on its own.

options.label: C
options.text: Put provisioning and configuration in separate repositories and rely on operators to keep the connection details in sync.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep resource provisioning in code, and document the manual software setup as the interface between the two.

grader_markdown: Provisioning establishes resources and connectivity; server configuration establishes software, files, and service state. Clear boundaries with explicit information flow support focused review and reuse. Separate repositories are optional and do not by themselves keep dependencies synchronized.

title: Dependencies and changing resource information
prompt_markdown: An application server requires a network. A later configuration step needs the server's assigned address, which may change when the server is replaced. The team currently copies that address into several files. Which design best preserves both dependency order and current connection information?

options.label: A
options.text: Declare the network-to-server and server-to-configuration dependencies, and derive the address from the current server output.

options.label: B
options.text: Number the definition files in deployment order, and keep the original address as a default value in each configuration file so it stays available.

options.label: C
options.text: Start the stages together, and keep retrying the configuration against the previously recorded address until the server becomes reachable.

options.label: D
options.text: Create the network and the server in order, and let each configuration stage keep its own reviewed copy of the address.

grader_markdown: Explicit dependencies identify what must exist or be known before another step can proceed. Passing current resource outputs avoids stale, duplicated addresses after replacement. File names alone do not encode those resource relationships, and correct ordering alone does not keep copied values current.

title: Shared definitions and environment differences
prompt_markdown: Development and production use copied infrastructure definitions. They should share an application structure, but production needs greater capacity. Independent edits have introduced differences whose purpose is unclear. Which approach best preserves legitimate differences and prevents accidental divergence?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the definitions separate and periodically copy production over development, using production capacity as the shared baseline.

options.label: B
options.text: Require identical definitions and values in both environments, and record production capacity changes in an operations checklist.

options.label: C
options.text: Share the common structure, keep environment-specific values explicit, and review today's differences against the intended design.

options.label: D
options.text: Create one shared definition, allow manual environment-specific changes after deployment, and review changes to the shared definition.

grader_markdown: A shared definition captures the common structure, while explicit environment values retain intended capacity differences. Compare definitions and actual state with the agreed design, then review and validate changes. Identical values are not required, and undocumented manual exceptions undermine the shared source of truth.

title: Image and running machine
prompt_markdown: What is the relationship between a machine image and a virtual machine?

options.label: A
options.text: The image is a live record of the machine's current CPU and memory usage.

options.label: B
options.text: Each image can start a single VM, so a second VM needs its own copy of the image.

options.label: C
options.text: When a running VM changes, those changes are usually written back to its source image.

options.label: D
options.text: One image can start many VMs, and each VM can then change independently.

grader_markdown: An image provides the starting state for multiple instances. The instances can change independently after launch; those changes do not automatically rewrite the image.

title: Image building and deployment
prompt_markdown: What distinguishes building a machine image from deploying machines based on that image?

options.label: A
options.text: Building creates a reusable artifact; deploying starts running machines from it.

options.label: B
options.text: Building a new image also updates the machines that were started from the old one.

options.label: C
options.text: Deploying a machine updates the shared source image whenever that machine changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Building an image removes the need for any instance-specific configuration at launch.

grader_markdown: Image building prepares a reusable artifact. Deployment uses that artifact to create running instances. Producing a new image does not automatically update existing machines or eliminate instance-specific initialization.

title: Rebuildability
prompt_markdown: The lecture describes a problematic form of a "golden image." What makes that example an anti-pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: The organization shares one base image across many teams and services.

options.label: B
options.text: The image is tested before use, which slows down releases.

options.label: C
options.text: It was changed by hand and cannot be rebuilt from a maintained definition.

options.label: D
options.text: The image is produced by an automated pipeline instead of by an administrator.

grader_markdown: The problem is hidden manual changes and the lack of a maintained, repeatable creation process. A shared baseline or an automated, rebuildable image is not inherently an anti-pattern, even if the team calls it a golden image.

title: Image compatibility
prompt_markdown: A team wants to use the same machine baseline on two virtualization platforms and on different processor architectures. Which assumption is sound?

options.label: A
options.text: A machine image can usually boot unchanged on any platform and processor architecture.

options.label: B
options.text: Check each platform and architecture; you may need separate image variants.

options.label: C
options.text: If the application name and version match, the machine images will be compatible.

options.label: D
options.text: The disk size is what decides whether an image can boot on a platform.

grader_markdown: Machine images must be compatible with the destination platform and processor architecture. A common intended baseline can require different artifacts or formats for different targets; the exact requirements depend on the target platforms.

title: Stock and custom images
prompt_markdown: An organization starts every server from a supplied stock image and repeats the same security and software setup at launch. What is the strongest reason to maintain a custom image?

options.label: A
options.text: It provides a tested company baseline, which reduces repeated setup but still needs maintenance.

options.label: B
options.text: It captures live application data, so separate data backups are no longer needed.

options.label: C
options.text: It picks up future security fixes as they are released, so its build definition can stay unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: It removes environment differences, so settings and machine identities should be built into it as well.

grader_markdown: A stock image is a supplied starting point. A custom image adds selected software and configuration, providing a tested baseline and reducing repeated initialization. It still requires maintenance, instance-specific settings, and separate protection of persistent data.

title: Build time and boot time
prompt_markdown: A fleet needs the same monitoring software on every machine, but each instance needs a distinct identity and environment-specific connection settings. Which division of work best fits image building and boot-time initialization?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the monitoring software and one shared machine identity in the image; change environment settings by hand after launch.

options.label: B
options.text: Install everything at boot time, because a reusable image cannot contain configured software.

options.label: C
options.text: Put the monitoring software in the image; supply identity and environment settings during boot-time initialization.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the production connection settings in each image, and keep boot-time initialization for a check that the machine boots.

grader_markdown: Build-time work becomes part of a reusable image; boot-time initialization can supply values specific to an instance or environment. Other divisions may be valid, but this one directly separates the stable shared baseline from the varying inputs. Boot-time initialization alone is not ongoing reconciliation.

title: Containers and virtual machines
prompt_markdown: Which statement correctly compares a typical Linux container with a virtual machine and identifies a consequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Containers and VMs both boot their own kernel, so they provide the same kernel isolation boundary.

options.label: B
options.text: Containers share the host kernel, so a process in one container can see and change files in another.

options.label: C
options.text: VMs run their own guest kernel, which means any VM image can run unchanged on every processor architecture and hypervisor.

options.label: D
options.text: Containers share the host kernel and VMs run their own, so a workload needing another kernel may need a VM.

grader_markdown: Typical Linux containers share a host kernel while isolating aspects of their execution environment. A VM has a guest kernel over virtualized hardware. Kernel sharing affects compatibility and isolation; neither approach guarantees that arbitrary images work on every platform.

title: Snapshot and rebuildable definition
prompt_markdown: A team has a snapshot of a working server but no maintained definition of how it was configured. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It records how the server was configured, so future changes can be reviewed from its creation history.

options.label: B
options.text: It can restore the captured state, yet a maintained definition is needed to review and rebuild the setup.

options.label: C
options.text: It is of no use for recovery, because restoring a machine requires a rebuildable definition.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that future builds will match the server, as long as the same stock image name is selected.

grader_markdown: A snapshot captures state at a point in time, within its scope and consistency limits. It can support restoration but does not explain the intended build process or make hidden manual changes reviewable. Rebuildable definitions and data backups serve different purposes.

title: Organizing an image family
prompt_markdown: Web-server and database-server images share a security baseline but need different software. Their separate build definitions contain copied baseline steps, and a policy update reached only one copy. Which plan best addresses both organization and rollout?

options.label: A
options.text: Build one image with both workloads installed, and apply baseline changes to whichever running servers currently need them.

options.label: B
options.text: Share a common baseline with separate workload definitions; committing a new baseline version also updates existing images and running machines.

options.label: C
options.text: Share a common baseline with separate workload definitions; rebuild affected images, test policy and workloads, then replace machines deliberately.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the copied baseline steps and review each copy, then validate the baseline definition before replacing machines from existing images.

grader_markdown: A shared baseline reduces inconsistent copies while workload-specific definitions preserve useful differences. Updating source does not update existing artifacts or instances: affected images must be rebuilt, tested, and deliberately rolled out. Validation should cover both the policy and the workloads.

title: Reproducible builds and immutable updates
prompt_markdown: A version-controlled image build always selects the latest base image and packages. The team wants to reproduce an approved version and later roll out a deliberately patched version. Which plan meets both goals?

options.label: A
options.text: Pin and keep the approved base image and packages; build and test a patched image, then replace instances while protecting persistent data.

options.label: B
options.text: Re-run the same source revision with the latest inputs, update existing servers in place, and call the unchanged source an immutable release.

options.label: C
options.text: Record the approved base image but keep selecting the latest packages, then replace the machines and rebuild their data from the build definition.

options.label: D
options.text: Control both base and package versions, patch running machines by hand, and rely on their original image for any future replacement.

grader_markdown: Version-controlled instructions do not freeze external inputs such as base images and packages, so reproduction requires controlled versions and available artifacts. The lecture treats a built image as a versioned artifact: keeping the previous version allows a rollback, and each new image is tested before release. An immutable update builds and validates a new image, replaces instances deliberately, and protects persistent data through separate storage or a verified copy, as in the lecture's case study where machines were replaced in minutes while their data was preserved.

title: Inventory
prompt_markdown: What is the main purpose of an inventory in server configuration management?

options.label: A
options.text: To store a complete binary snapshot of each managed server

options.label: B
options.text: To list managed hosts and groups and attach targeting information to them

options.label: C
options.text: To replace reusable configuration definitions with a separate list of settings for each host

options.label: D
options.text: To record which operations failed during the previous run

grader_markdown: An inventory identifies target hosts and groups and can associate relevant information with them. It supports selecting the appropriate targets for configuration; it is not a complete backup of their state.

title: Partial state management
prompt_markdown: An automation system manages only the resources explicitly declared to it. Its declaration requires a web service but says nothing about an unrelated package installed manually. What should you expect after a successful run?

options.label: A
options.text: Every package not named in the declaration is removed automatically during the run.

options.label: B
options.text: The machine is recreated from a stock image so that it matches the declaration.

options.label: C
options.text: The successful run shows the whole machine now matches a complete baseline.

options.label: D
options.text: The package can stay, as the automation never touches what it was not told to manage.

grader_markdown: The system in the question manages explicitly declared resources. A resource outside that scope is not automatically declared absent, so unmanaged state can remain even after successful configuration.

title: Reusable configuration units
prompt_markdown: What is the strongest reason to organize server configuration into reusable units for common setup, web services, and databases?

options.label: A
options.text: It groups related work so each part can be understood, reused and maintained.

options.label: B
options.text: It guarantees that the configuration actions can run at the same time.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes each unit independent of the other resources and inputs it might use.

options.label: D
options.text: It removes the need to test how the units behave when combined on one server.

grader_markdown: Grouping related responsibilities creates units that can be understood, reused, and maintained. Such units can still have dependencies and need integration testing; splitting files does not guarantee independence or parallelism.

title: Agent-based and agentless tools
prompt_markdown: A team manages a fleet of servers with a configuration tool. What is the main practical difference between an agentless tool and an agent-based one?

options.label: A
options.text: Agentless tools connect over an existing protocol such as SSH; agent-based tools need software on every node.

options.label: B
options.text: Agentless tools cannot be idempotent, because checking a node's state before changing it needs an agent running there.

options.label: C
options.text: Agentless tools need no network access to the managed nodes, while agent-based tools do.

options.label: D
options.text: Agent-based tools are limited to Windows machines, while agentless tools are limited to Linux.

grader_markdown: Agentless tools reach nodes through protocols that are already available, typically SSH or WinRM, so nothing extra has to be installed. Agent-based tools need an agent on each node, which can then apply configuration on its own schedule. Both kinds can be idempotent, both rely on network connectivity, and neither is limited to one operating system.

title: Grouping by responsibility
prompt_markdown: Web, database, and batch-processing servers all need a common baseline but different workload configuration. Which organization expresses both requirements with the least duplicated baseline logic?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep a complete copy of the baseline in each workload group, so each team can change its own copy freely.

options.label: B
options.text: Apply every configuration unit to every server, and let operators disable the unwanted services afterwards.

options.label: C
options.text: Use workload groups for connection settings, and put the whole server configuration into one sequence that runs on every host.

options.label: D
options.text: Apply one reusable baseline to the whole fleet, and select workload-specific units through the matching host groups.

grader_markdown: Grouping selects the appropriate targets; reusable units define the configuration to apply. Composing a common baseline with workload-specific units avoids both duplicated baseline logic and installation of every workload on every host. No particular inventory syntax or folder layout is required.

title: Desired state and operational actions
prompt_markdown: A service is already running and its relevant configuration has not changed. How does declaring that it should be running differ from requesting a restart on every automation run?

options.label: A
options.text: Both requests stop and start the service again, because automation cannot confirm a running state without restarting it.

options.label: B
options.text: The declaration takes effect on the first deployment, after which a restart request is needed to recover from a later failure.

options.label: C
options.text: The declaration can leave the healthy service alone, while an unconditional restart disrupts it on every run.

options.label: D
options.text: The restart request becomes a no-op after its first success, even though the automation repeats it on later runs.

grader_markdown: A running-state declaration describes a condition that may already hold. A restart request describes an operation. Repeated execution can therefore leave a healthy service undisturbed with the first approach and disrupt it with the second. Relevant changes can still justify a restart.

title: Responding to configuration changes
prompt_markdown: Several compatible configuration changes must be applied before a service reloads them. Which approach best avoids unnecessary work while activating a coherent configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Reload after each file is copied, even when its contents did not change, so each step is visible on its own.

options.label: B
options.text: Apply and validate all the changes, then reload once if relevant configuration actually changed.

options.label: C
options.text: Reload before changing the files, then skip the final reload if the configuration steps report success.

options.label: D
options.text: Apply the changes and skip the reload while the service keeps running, since a running process reads new settings by itself.

grader_markdown: Apply and validate compatible changes before activation, then reload when relevant state changed. This avoids repeated reloads and allows the service to consume a coherent configuration. A running process does not necessarily reread changed files automatically.

title: Configuration success and functional success
prompt_markdown: All configuration steps report success, but users cannot use the application. Which interpretation and follow-up check are most useful?

options.label: A
options.text: Successful configuration means the application works; compare the automation exit codes from two consecutive runs.

options.label: B
options.text: The deployment must have drifted; check whether the expected configuration files still exist.

options.label: C
options.text: Configuration can succeed while the application fails; send a representative request through it and its dependencies.

options.label: D
options.text: A running service shows the application is reachable; compare installed package names with the deployment log.

grader_markdown: Configuration checks establish selected resource conditions, not necessarily end-to-end behavior. A representative request can expose failures in connectivity, dependencies, or application behavior that file, package, and process checks miss. Configuration success and functional failure can coexist.

title: Comparing codebase organizations
prompt_markdown: A growing team is considering replacing one large configuration file with reusable units and explicit environment composition. Which proposal best balances reuse with the cost of added structure?

options.label: A
options.text: Split each operation into its own unit and select units implicitly; the large number of files makes ownership and the effective configuration self-explanatory.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy each environment into its own repository; independent changes remove the need to coordinate common behavior across environments.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep one universal unit and add environment conditions throughout it; using a single file removes the need to document how environment values interact.

options.label: D
options.text: Use coherent baseline and workload units with documented inputs and override rules, and test how they combine, since added interfaces can hide conflicts.

grader_markdown: Coherent units support reuse and focused review, but extra interfaces and indirection can obscure dependencies and effective values. Documented inputs, visible composition, clear override rules, and integration checks address those costs. A small system may still be adequately served by a single file.

title: Checking the intended state
prompt_markdown: A deployment skips software setup whenever an 'application' directory exists. The directory remains after the desired version changes, so the process reports success without inspecting the version or behavior. Which correction best establishes the intended state?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the directory check but run the process twice; two unchanged runs show that the desired version is installed.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare the installed version with the desired one, fix any mismatch, then check the version and the application's behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: Recreate the directory on each run, and treat its new timestamp as proof that the application has been updated.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the desired version to the deployment log whenever the directory exists, and use that log as the check on future runs.

grader_markdown: Directory existence is not evidence of the desired software version or a complete installation. Repeated no-ops can preserve an incorrect state. Compare meaningful observed state with intended state, update when needed, and verify the result; changing a timestamp or log does not establish actual configuration.

title: Chaos engineering
prompt_markdown: What is the main purpose of chaos engineering practices, such as randomly terminating servers in a running system?

options.label: A
options.text: To cut cloud costs by finding servers that have no remaining users and can be deleted

options.label: B
options.text: To identify who owns each server, by waiting to see which team complains after it stops

options.label: C
options.text: To show, again and again, that the system recovers from failures without users noticing

options.label: D
options.text: To reduce the need for monitoring, since failures introduced on purpose need no alerts

grader_markdown: Chaos engineering deliberately introduces failures, such as terminating servers or whole zones, to prove continuously that automated recovery works and that users do not notice. Stopping a server to find its owner is the scream test, not chaos engineering. Deliberate failures depend on monitoring and alerting rather than replacing them.

title: Regions and availability zones
prompt_markdown: A service must stay available if one data center in a cloud region fails. Which placement fits the lecture's description of regions and availability zones?

options.label: A
options.text: Spread instances across availability zones, which are separate data centers in one region

options.label: B
options.text: Put the instances in one availability zone, since each zone already spans several regions

options.label: C
options.text: Use a different region for each instance, because zones in a region usually share a building

options.label: D
options.text: Add instances inside one zone, since extra capacity there gives the same failure protection

grader_markdown: A region is a geographic location; its availability zones are physically separate data centers located close to each other. Placing instances in different zones lets the service survive the loss of one data center. Extra instances in a single zone share that zone's failure, and moving every instance to a different region is not needed for this goal.

title: Scream test
prompt_markdown: An engineer finds a server that seems unused, has no known owner, and receives almost no traffic. What does a "scream test" involve?

options.label: A
options.text: Deleting the server and its backups at once, since unused infrastructure only adds cost

options.label: B
options.text: Sending a burst of traffic to it to check whether it survives a sudden spike in load

options.label: C
options.text: Rebuilding it from code under a new name, so that its owner can be identified later

options.label: D
options.text: Stopping the server for a while and waiting to see whether anyone reports a problem

grader_markdown: A scream test stops, rather than deletes, seemingly unused infrastructure and waits to see whether anyone complains. Silence suggests the resource is unused; a complaint identifies a dependency or owner. Because the resource is only stopped, it can be brought back. The same approach can also check whether monitoring and alerting notice the outage.

title: Organizing a growing playbook
prompt_markdown: A single playbook has grown to several hundred lines. It configures web servers, databases, and batch jobs, and a service's restart handler is defined far from the tasks that notify it. Which reorganization fits the lecture's advice?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep one file so every dependency stays visible, and add comments that link tasks to handlers

options.label: B
options.text: Split it into roles or included files that each fit in your head, grouping what changes together

options.label: C
options.text: Split it into one file per task so each file stays short, even if handlers end up far from tasks

options.label: D
options.text: Copy it into one repository per server type, so each copy can shrink as the copies diverge

grader_markdown: The instructor's rule of thumb is to work on code that fits in your head. When a playbook grows to several hundred lines, split it into included task files or roles, separate concerns such as web servers, databases, and batch jobs, and keep things that change for the same reason, such as a service's tasks and its handler, close together. Comments do not reduce the size, one file per task scatters related parts, and per-type copies duplicate code that then diverges.

title: Testing from a clean state
prompt_markdown: A developer tests a provisioning definition by applying each new change to the same long-lived test machine. Every run passes, but the first run on a new machine fails. Which explanation and practice are most useful?

options.label: A
options.text: The new machine has drifted; recreate it from a snapshot of the test machine and run again

options.label: B
options.text: Earlier runs left state that the code needs but never creates; also test it from a clean state

options.label: C
options.text: The code is not idempotent; run it twice on the test machine to show it will work anywhere

options.label: D
options.text: New machines may be slower to start; add retries and waits, as the code works on the test machine

grader_markdown: Repeatedly applying changes to one machine accumulates state, so a step that only worked because of earlier leftovers can go unnoticed. Testing regularly from an empty state, as well as on an already provisioned machine, shows the code works on any compatible new machine. Running twice on the same machine or adding retries does not reveal the missing step.

title: Restart tests
prompt_markdown: Provisioning completes and the application responds. Why is it also worth testing that the machine and its services still work after a restart?

options.label: A
options.text: A restart is the most reliable way to apply configuration, so each run should end with one

options.label: B
options.text: A restart resets the machine to its image, which shows whether provisioning is still needed

options.label: C
options.text: A clean boot can stand in for functional checks, as a machine that starts usually serves users

options.label: D
options.text: Services can work after provisioning yet fail after a reboot; a tested restart can be automated

grader_markdown: A service can be configured and running yet fail to come back after a reboot or service restart. Testing restarts shows the provisioned setup is valid beyond the first run. Once restarts are known to work, monitoring can restart unresponsive servers automatically. A restart does not replace functional checks, and it does not reset a machine to its image.

title: Changes reported on every run
prompt_markdown: On every run against an already provisioned server, two tasks report a change to the same directory: one sets its owner to one user, the other to a different user. What is the best diagnosis and fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Two tasks manage one resource in conflicting ways; give the directory one intended state

options.label: B
options.text: The changes may be harmless if the run succeeds, so they can be ignored once the server works

options.label: C
options.text: The server drifts after each run; rebuild it from a fresh image before the next run starts

options.label: D
options.text: Add a service restart at the end of the run so the service picks up the owner set last

grader_markdown: When two tasks set the same resource to different states, each run undoes the other and reports a change, so the definition never converges. Giving the directory one intended state, managed in one place, restores a clean re-run with no changes. Ignoring constant changes hides real problems, and rebuilding or restarting does not remove the conflict in the code.

title: Guardrails for generated code
prompt_markdown: A team uses an AI coding assistant to generate infrastructure code. Which approach gives the most dependable evidence that the generated code meets the team's goals?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the same assistant to confirm its output, since it can explain the reasoning behind it

options.label: B
options.text: Run the code once in one environment; if it works there, it can usually be trusted elsewhere

options.label: C
options.text: Define acceptance tests and policies, and iterate on the code until all of them pass

options.label: D
options.text: Use the most capable model available, since its output rarely needs tests or review

grader_markdown: Acceptance criteria expressed as tests and policies act as guardrails: generated code is revised until it passes them, which the lecture calls loop engineering. Self-confirmation by the same assistant, a single successful run in one environment, or trust in a stronger model do not show that the code meets the requirements. The team still needs to understand the tests and the code.

title: Changing production without disruption
prompt_markdown: A web shop announces multi-hour maintenance windows for each release and avoids changes on Fridays, because losing a production server would be a disaster. The team wants to make routine changes during working hours without users noticing. Which plan best fits the principles from the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Make servers rebuildable from code, spread them across zones, rehearse failures, and deploy without downtime

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the maintenance windows but shorten them, and require two engineers to approve any change that is made on a Friday

options.label: C
options.text: Take more frequent snapshots of the production servers, and restore them by hand whenever a release causes an outage

options.label: D
options.text: Start terminating random production servers straight away, and add monitoring later if users begin to report failures

grader_markdown: When servers can be rebuilt from code, are spread across availability zones, and are monitored, losing one is not a disaster. Rehearsing failures, as in chaos engineering, proves that recovery works, and zero-downtime methods such as blue-green deployment keep changes invisible to users. Maintenance windows and Friday rules work around missing automation, manual snapshot restores keep the outage, and chaos without monitoring is reckless.

title: Acting on an AI code review
prompt_markdown: An AI assistant reviewed a playbook it helped write. It reported a private key committed to the repository, a bug that leaves the application stopped after a restart, and a shell command used where a state-aware module now exists. Unasked, it also split the small playbook into many files. Which response is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Accept all of the changes as generated, including the new file layout, because the review found the problems by itself

options.label: B
options.text: Make the repository private so the key can stay, fix the bug by hand, and keep the shell command because it already works

options.label: C
options.text: Set the findings aside, because the playbook completed without errors and a successful run usually means the code is correct

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the key from version control, fix the bug with a test that reproduces it, use the module, and undo the needless split

grader_markdown: Secrets such as private keys do not belong in version control, even in a private repository. A bug found in review should be fixed together with a test that would have caught it, so it cannot silently return. A module with built-in state management is more reliable than a shell command with a guard. AI suggestions still need review: an unrequested split of a small playbook adds structure without benefit.

title: Looking up existing resources
prompt_markdown: A provisioning definition needs the ID of a shared network and the most recent approved base image. Another team maintains both. What does a read-only data lookup of these objects do?

options.label: A
options.text: It imports both objects, so later runs of this definition will manage and update them.

options.label: B
options.text: It reads current details of objects managed elsewhere, without creating, changing or deleting them.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates private copies of the network and image, so the two teams no longer depend on each other.

options.label: D
options.text: It records the values on the first run, so later runs usually keep using that original image.

grader_markdown: A data lookup queries information about an object that already exists and is managed somewhere else, such as a shared network or the latest matching image. The definition can then use that information, but the tool does not take ownership of the object or create, change or delete it. The lookup runs again on later runs, so a "latest" query can return a newer image.

title: Removing a resource from the definition
prompt_markdown: A team uses a provisioning tool that records the resources it created in a state file. They delete one server's definition from the code and apply again, changing nothing else. What should they expect?

options.label: A
options.text: The server stays running, because removing its definition just means the tool stops managing it.

options.label: B
options.text: The tool deletes every server in the account that does not appear in the current definitions.

options.label: C
options.text: The apply fails until someone deletes the server by hand and then removes its state entry.

options.label: D
options.text: The tool finds the server in its state but not in the code, and plans to destroy it.

grader_markdown: A tool that keeps state compares the code, the recorded state and the real infrastructure. A resource that is recorded in state but missing from the code is treated as no longer wanted, so the plan proposes destroying it. Resources the tool never created are not in its state and are left alone. Leaving the server running is the behavior of a tool that manages only what is currently declared.

title: Provider plugins
prompt_markdown: One project manages virtual machines in a public cloud, records at a separate DNS provider, and alert rules in a monitoring service. What makes this possible with a single declarative tool?

options.label: A
options.text: Provider plugins expose each service's API as resource types, so one project can combine them.

options.label: B
options.text: The tool manages other services once the cloud vendor has added them to its own API.

options.label: C
options.text: Each service needs a separate project, because a single run cannot combine several providers.

options.label: D
options.text: The tool signs in to each web console and repeats the clicks an administrator would make.

grader_markdown: Provider plugins translate declared resources into calls to a particular service's API. Because providers are independent, one project and one run can combine resources from a cloud, a DNS provider, a CDN or a monitoring service. The large community library of providers is a main reason such tools are widely used. They work through APIs, not by automating web consoles.

title: Diagram boxes and planned resources
prompt_markdown: An architecture diagram shows a load balancer, a group of database nodes, and a front end. The provisioning plan lists sixteen resources to add. What best explains the difference?

options.label: A
options.text: The tool usually adds a hidden backup copy of each resource, so that rollback is possible.

options.label: B
options.text: The plan lists each attribute of a resource, such as its size or tags, as a separate resource.

options.label: C
options.text: The tool mirrors the provider's model, where one box can need several API objects.

options.label: D
options.text: The plan counts each resource twice, so just eight of them will actually be created.

grader_markdown: A declarative provisioning tool reflects the resource model of the provider it talks to. One diagram box, such as a load balancer, can need several API objects: the balancer, a listener, a target group and one attachment per node, plus firewall rules and keys. The complexity comes from the provider's model, so you need to understand that model to write the definition.

title: Sharing state in a team
prompt_markdown: A provisioning project's state lives on one engineer's laptop and covers the whole platform. Eight people now change the networks, databases and application servers at different rates. Which approach best fits the lecture's guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Give each engineer a personal copy of the state, and merge the copies at the end of each week.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep one state for everything in the code repository, so that reviews also show its changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the state before each run, so the tool rebuilds its knowledge from the account every time.

options.label: D
options.text: Use shared protected state, one run per state at a time, and split states by layer and change rate.

grader_markdown: When several people share a project, state should live in shared storage rather than on one laptop, and only one run should change a given state at a time. Splitting state by layer and frequency of change reduces waiting and limits how much each run can affect. State can contain sensitive values, such as a generated private key, so it needs protection. Personal copies or a deleted state lose track of what the tool created.

title: Competing rule definitions
prompt_markdown: A firewall group is defined with its rules written inline. A colleague adds more rules for the same group as separate rule resources. Each apply now reports changes, although nobody edited the code. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Two definitions compete for the same rules; choose one modeling style for that group.

options.label: B
options.text: The provider is reporting a temporary fault, and retrying the apply a few times usually settles it.

options.label: C
options.text: The account has drifted on its own, and refreshing the state once will stop the repeated changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Separate rule resources take priority over inline rules, so the colleague's rules win.

grader_markdown: Some providers let you model the same thing as nested blocks inside a resource or as separate resources linked to it. Using both for one group means two definitions claim the same rules, so each apply undoes the other's result and a change loop follows. Pick one style for that group; the lecture noted that the separate-resource style is now preferred for this case.

title: Create-time provisioning scripts
prompt_markdown: A server definition includes a script that installs and configures software when the server is first created. Later, the team edits the script to change a setting. What should they expect, and what fits larger setups?

options.label: A
options.text: Existing servers are updated in place on the next apply, and inline scripts scale well to large setups.

options.label: B
options.text: The tool reruns every script on each apply, so the scripts need to be safe to repeat on every server.

options.label: C
options.text: Existing servers keep the old setup, as the script ran only at creation; big setups can use a configuration tool.

options.label: D
options.text: The next apply fails, because a script attached to a resource is locked once that resource has been created.

grader_markdown: A create-time provisioning script runs when the resource is created and is not rerun on later applies while the resource exists, so editing it does not change existing servers. Such scripts mix imperative steps into a declarative definition. They can work for small setups, but larger ones can keep the provisioning tool for machines and use a configuration tool, or a prebuilt image, for the software inside them.

title: Reviewing destructive plan entries
prompt_markdown: After a small change, the preview reports six resources to add and three to destroy. Which response is most appropriate before approving the apply?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve it, because a plan that also adds new resources will recreate anything that it destroys.

options.label: B
options.text: Check what would be destroyed and why; replacing a helper that holds no data can be harmless.

options.label: C
options.text: Cancel it, since any plan that destroys resources means that the code was changed incorrectly.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip the preview next time and apply directly, because a preview may list changes that will not happen.

grader_markdown: A plan is a preview, so use it to check what each destroy or replace entry refers to and why it happens. In the lecture, the destroyed items were helper resources that only ran commands and could only be replaced, so recreating them lost nothing. Destroying a resource that holds data or serves traffic needs much more care. Destroy entries are not automatically wrong, and adding resources does not undo a deletion.

title: Clients and a changing group of nodes
prompt_markdown: A search cluster runs on several nodes. Its web front end is configured with the address of each node. Adding a node means reconfiguring the front end, and when a node fails, some requests still reach it. Which design best addresses both problems?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the node list in the front end, generate it from provisioning outputs, and redeploy the front end after each change.

options.label: B
options.text: Give each node a public address and publish the list, so that users can pick a responsive node themselves.

options.label: C
options.text: Put a load balancer with health checks in front of the nodes, and point the front end at its stable address.

options.label: D
options.text: Run larger nodes, which can make failures less likely, and keep the front end configured with the node addresses.

grader_markdown: A load balancer gives clients one stable endpoint, so nodes can be added or replaced without reconfiguring the front end. Its health checks take failing nodes out of rotation, so requests stop reaching them. It can also absorb traffic spikes. Generating the node list automatically still needs a redeploy on each change and does nothing about failures. Larger nodes do not remove failures, and publishing node addresses pushes the problem onto users.

title: Rerunning derived configuration
prompt_markdown: Each node in a cluster needs a file listing all cluster members. A separate step generates and copies that file, and it reruns only when the node it targets changes. After the cluster grows from three to four nodes, the plan copies the file only to the new node. What is the best correction?

options.label: A
options.text: Make the step rerun whenever the set of members changes, so every node receives the updated list.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the step as it is, because existing nodes can usually discover a new member without help.

options.label: C
options.text: Recreate the four nodes on every apply, so that each one starts with a fresh file.

options.label: D
options.text: Copy the updated file to the existing nodes by hand after each scale-up, and note it in the runbook.

grader_markdown: The file depends on the whole membership, so the step should rerun when the membership changes, for example by including the node identifiers in what triggers it. Every node then gets the updated list, not only the new one. The lecture's plan revealed this mistake before it was applied. Recreating all nodes on every run is disruptive, manual copying breaks reproducibility, and assuming automatic discovery ignores how the cluster is configured.

title: Paying for functions
prompt_markdown: A team deploys a scheduled job on a function-as-a-service platform. For most of the month nothing invokes it. How is its compute typically charged under the model described in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: By the execution time and memory used, so idle periods add no compute charge.

options.label: B
options.text: By the hour from deployment, as with a virtual machine, whether or not it runs.

options.label: C
options.text: By a flat monthly fee for each function that is deployed on the platform.

options.label: D
options.text: By the size of the deployed code package, regardless of how often it is called.

grader_markdown: Function-as-a-service platforms charge for the compute actually used while code runs, measured by execution time and allocated memory. A deployed function that is not invoked adds no compute charge. This makes functions very cheap for low or sporadic load, although high sustained traffic can make them expensive.

title: Packaging as container images
prompt_markdown: The instructor prefers packaging applications as container images, even where a function platform can also run a plain code archive. What is the main reason given?

options.label: A
options.text: Container images remove the need to grant runtime permissions to the application.

options.label: B
options.text: A container image is usually cheaper to store in a registry than a code archive.

options.label: C
options.text: One image can run as a function, on a container service, or on a VM with little change.

options.label: D
options.text: Container images make the application immune to differences between cloud providers.

grader_markdown: A container image is a portable package: the same image can run as a function, on a container service, or on a VM, so changing the platform does not mean repackaging the application. The image may need small adjustments for a particular platform. It does not remove permission needs or provider differences, and storage cost is not the reason given.

title: DNS under infrastructure as code
prompt_markdown: An organization wants its public DNS setup managed as infrastructure as code. Which division of responsibility matches the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep DNS records manual, because DNS providers rarely offer an API for automation.

options.label: B
options.text: Buy the domain outside the code; manage its records as code through the provider's API.

options.label: C
options.text: Manage records as code only when DNS is hosted by the same cloud as the application.

options.label: D
options.text: Include the domain purchase in the code, so that a destroy run also gives up the domain.

grader_markdown: Purchasing a domain is usually a one-time business action outside infrastructure code. The DNS records, whether hosted by the cloud provider or an external DNS service, are managed through an API and can be defined and reviewed as code. Hosting DNS with another provider does not prevent this.

title: Small code change, large cost change
prompt_markdown: A teammate approves enabling a load balancer because the change adds only a few lines of infrastructure code. What else should the review consider?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing more, since a short change to a definition has a similarly small effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Mainly the formatting, since cost questions can usually be left to the billing team.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether traffic is high today, since a load balancer with no traffic is free of charge.

options.label: D
options.text: The running cost, since a load balancer can be billed monthly even with no traffic.

grader_markdown: A design change that looks small in code can change the running cost a lot. A load balancer is billed for as long as it exists, even with no traffic, while a function URL or direct public address may cost little or nothing. Reviewers should weigh the cost and the traffic actually expected, not just the size of the diff.

title: Where scheduling lives
prompt_markdown: A batch job runs for a few minutes each hour. Design 1 keeps a container running all the time and lets the application decide when to start the job. Design 2 uses an external scheduler that starts the job on demand. Which comparison is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Design 1 is cheaper, since starting work on demand costs more than keeping one container running.

options.label: B
options.text: Both use the same compute, since the platform bills for the schedule rather than running time.

options.label: C
options.text: Design 2 uses compute only while the job runs; design 1 uses it for the whole time it stays up.

options.label: D
options.text: Design 2 needs no permissions setup, since the platform scheduler can start any job by itself.

grader_markdown: A container that runs all the time and handles its own schedule uses compute for its whole lifetime, even between jobs. Moving the scheduling to an external service or timer means the job runs, and is paid for, only when needed. The scheduler still needs explicit permission to start the job.

title: Console defaults and explicit definitions
prompt_markdown: A function created by hand in the web console wrote logs without any extra setup. The same function, recreated from infrastructure code, runs but writes no logs. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: Functions created from code cannot write logs, so a logging agent has to be installed.

options.label: B
options.text: The console added default permissions and resources that the code must declare explicitly.

options.label: C
options.text: Logs from code-created functions may be delayed by a day, so waiting is usually enough.

options.label: D
options.text: The code-created function runs on a VM, so its logs stay on that machine's local disk.

grader_markdown: Web consoles often create supporting resources and permissions, such as permission to write logs, automatically. Infrastructure code creates only what it declares, so the role, its permissions, and the log group must be defined explicitly. This makes the setup visible and reviewable but means console defaults cannot be assumed.

title: Secrets in automated deployments
prompt_markdown: An application needs a database password at runtime. The infrastructure tool keeps a state record of the resources it manages. Which approach best follows the lecture's guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Set the password as an environment value in the definition, as the state sits in a private bucket.

options.label: B
options.text: Build the password into the container image, so the definition and state can leave it out.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the password in state on purpose, so the tool can notice when someone changes it.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the value out of state, pass the app the secret's name, and let it read only that secret.

grader_markdown: Secret values should not be written into the tool's state or into plain configuration, where anyone with access to them could read the secret. Store the value in a secrets service, give the application only a reference such as the secret's name, and grant its identity read access to that specific secret. Baking secrets into images or relying on a private state bucket still spreads the value.

title: What a lower-level service asks of you
prompt_markdown: A team moves the same web application from a function service with a built-in URL to a container service. Which extra infrastructure will they most likely have to define?

options.label: A
options.text: Network placement and firewall rules, because the containers get addresses in a network.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing extra, because both services hide networking and expose a public URL by default.

options.label: C
options.text: A Kubernetes cluster, because a container service can only run containers inside one.

options.label: D
options.text: Host operating-system patching, because the container service may expose its VMs to the team.

grader_markdown: A function service with a built-in URL handles networking for you. A container service is a lower-level service: containers get addresses inside a network, so the team must choose the network and subnets and define firewall rules, or the containers cannot be reached. The provider still manages the hosts, and no Kubernetes cluster is needed.

title: Choosing a compute platform
prompt_markdown: A small company runs a web app that gets a handful of requests per hour, with occasional short spikes, plus a background job that runs for a few minutes every hour. Both parts are small and already packaged as container images. The company has a tight budget and no existing Kubernetes platform. Which deployment best fits the trade-offs discussed in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: A managed Kubernetes cluster behind a load balancer, since a cluster is the usual way to run two containers.

options.label: B
options.text: Functions for both parts, a scheduled event for the job, and the function URL instead of a load balancer.

options.label: C
options.text: An always-on container service for both parts behind a load balancer, keeping spare capacity for spikes.

options.label: D
options.text: One large VM sized for the biggest spike, since a VM is usually cheaper than functions for low traffic.

grader_markdown: With low, bursty traffic and a short periodic job, pay-per-execution functions scale with demand and cost almost nothing while idle. A scheduled event starts the job only when needed, and the built-in function URL avoids the fixed cost of a load balancer. A cluster, always-on containers, or a VM sized for peak load all pay for idle capacity, which is hard to justify on a tight budget without an existing platform.

title: Organizing alternative deployments
prompt_markdown: A team keeps three versions of one deployment (functions, a container service, and a VM) as separate infrastructure projects that all use the same image registry. Only some setups need a load balancer, and each apply currently builds and pushes the images. Which organization is most suitable?

options.label: A
options.text: Give each project its own registry copy, enable the load balancer in every setup, and keep the image builds in the apply.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge all three versions into one project to share the registry, and comment out the load balancer where it is not needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the registry in a shared project, add an off-by-default load balancer toggle, and build images in a separate script.

options.label: D
options.text: Let each project create the registry when it is missing, and switch the load balancer on whenever traffic might need it.

grader_markdown: A resource used by several projects, such as a shared registry, is best managed once in its own project, with each deployment referring to it. A toggle that is off by default makes the costly load balancer an explicit, reviewable choice instead of manual commenting or a vague rule. Building and pushing images is an imperative build step, so a separate script or pipeline keeps the infrastructure definition focused on the desired state.

title: Integration tests for infrastructure code
prompt_markdown: Why does the lecture value integration tests on real targets more than unit tests for infrastructure code?

options.label: A
options.text: Unit tests usually run too slowly to fit into a delivery pipeline for infrastructure code.

options.label: B
options.text: Integration tests also check style and conventions, so a separate linter is no longer needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Unit tests cannot be written for infrastructure code in any of the common tools.

options.label: D
options.text: Most failures appear only when code meets a real system and its packages and services.

grader_markdown: Infrastructure code mostly orchestrates real systems, so its typical failures appear only when it runs against a target: different distributions ship different packages, paths, and service behavior. Unit tests can be written, but they exercise little of that. Integration tests do not replace linters, which catch a different class of problems before anything runs.

title: Module interface
prompt_markdown: In the lecture's view, what forms the interface of a reusable infrastructure module?

options.label: A
options.text: The full set of resources it creates, which callers edit directly when they need changes

options.label: B
options.text: The input parameters it publishes, with defaults, that callers set to adjust its behavior

options.label: C
options.text: The folder layout of its source files, which callers copy into their own projects

options.label: D
options.text: The commit history of its repository, which callers usually read to learn how to use it

grader_markdown: A module's published parameters and their defaults are how users interact with it: defaults give a working result, and overridable inputs act as extension points. The internal resources and file layout are implementation details that callers should not need to edit or copy. Commit history explains changes but is not the interface.

title: Linters
prompt_markdown: An automation tool already refuses to run a definition with invalid syntax. What does adding a linter contribute?

options.label: A
options.text: It replaces integration tests, since a definition that passes linting will behave correctly on real targets.

options.label: B
options.text: It runs the definition against a temporary machine and reports which resources failed to start.

options.label: C
options.text: It flags valid code that is risky or breaks agreed rules, such as a value parsed as an unexpected type.

options.label: D
options.text: It can repeat the tool's syntax check earlier, but it usually reports nothing the tool would accept.

grader_markdown: The tool's own parser already rejects invalid syntax. A linter applies further rules to code that is syntactically valid, catching risky constructs, convention violations, deprecated usage, or ambiguous values such as a number that some parsers read as a string. It is a static check and does not replace running the code on real targets.

title: Modules as maintained products
prompt_markdown: A team plans to extract repeated infrastructure code into a module that other teams will use. Which view matches the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: A shared module is a product needing tests, docs and releases; it pays off as complexity and teams grow.

options.label: B
options.text: A module is mainly a way to shorten files, so it needs no separate testing once the original code worked.

options.label: C
options.text: Every project should start with modules, because modules have no maintenance cost compared with plain code.

options.label: D
options.text: Modules mostly pay off for code published to public registries, much less for structure inside one company.

grader_markdown: The lecture treats a shared module as a software product: good modules need tests, documentation, examples, a release process, and ongoing effort. That cost is justified as infrastructure complexity and the number of teams grow, because modules also make delegation and knowledge transfer easier. Small setups may not need modules, and modules are also useful inside one organization.

title: Order of pipeline checks
prompt_markdown: A delivery pipeline for infrastructure code runs linting, policy checks, smoke tests, a staging deployment with integration tests, and then production. Why are the static checks placed first?

options.label: A
options.text: They catch many problems in seconds, before slower stages spend time or create real resources.

options.label: B
options.text: They can find every problem a staging deployment would find, so later stages rarely fail.

options.label: C
options.text: Production approval usually depends on how many lint warnings were fixed, more than on test results.

options.label: D
options.text: Passing them first lets the later stages skip their own checks and finish the release faster.

grader_markdown: Linting and policy checks are fast and need no infrastructure, so placing them first gives quick feedback and stops obvious problems before costly stages create resources. They cannot replace deployment and integration tests, which find problems that only appear on real targets. Each stage still runs its own checks.

title: Assessing a third-party module
prompt_markdown: A team finds a public module that does what it needs. Which assessment best fits the lecture's advice before depending on it?

options.label: A
options.text: Prefer the module with the most parameters, since a larger interface usually signals higher quality.

options.label: B
options.text: Use it if its download count is high, because popularity shows it was tested on your platforms.

options.label: C
options.text: Check recent releases, issue fixes, and docs; if it looks inactive, consider insourcing a copy.

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid public modules entirely, because code written by outsiders cannot be reviewed or adapted.

grader_markdown: Signs of a healthy module include recent releases, active issue and security fixing, an evolving interface, and good documentation and examples. If a module looks inactive, its code can still be insourced, adapted, and maintained by the team. Download counts mostly reflect how widely the underlying software is used, not that the module was tested on your platforms; the number of parameters is not a quality measure either.

title: Providers and modules
prompt_markdown: A team wants to manage a new cloud service with code and also standardize how other teams use it. Which split of responsibilities matches the lecture's layering?

options.label: A
options.text: Write a module that calls the service's API directly, and use a provider only to store shared default values.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a provider for the service's API, and build a module that combines its resources into a reusable unit.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the cloud vendor for a module, since providers are usually written by each team for its own project.

options.label: D
options.text: Treat provider and module as two names for the same layer, so either one can hold the team's conventions.

grader_markdown: A provider, or a library of tasks, is the integration layer that turns definitions into API calls for a platform. A module sits one level higher: it combines those resources with the organization's choices into a reusable unit with an interface. Conventions belong in the module, not in the provider.

title: Policy as code
prompt_markdown: A security team wants every infrastructure project to tag resources with their environment and to stay below an agreed instance size. The code is syntactically valid and passes linting. Which approach fits best?

options.label: A
options.text: Rely on reviewers to remember the rules, since automated checks can only find syntax errors.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the rules as comments in each module, so users can read them before applying changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Wait for monitoring to report oversized or untagged resources after they reach production.

options.label: D
options.text: Define the rules once as policies and check them in every project's pipeline before release.

grader_markdown: Rules such as required tags, size limits, or approved providers are valid code from the tool's and linter's point of view, so they need a policy engine. Defining them once as policy as code lets the same organization-wide rules run automatically in every project's pipeline and block a release that violates them. Comments and reviewer memory are not enforced, and monitoring catches the problem only after it has reached production.

title: Adopting a breaking module release
prompt_markdown: Staging and production both use version 1.8.2 of a shared network module. Version 2.0.0 adds a feature the team needs and renames some inputs. How should the consuming team adopt it?

options.label: A
options.text: Point both environments at the latest release, apply to production first since it needs the feature most, then fix staging.

options.label: B
options.text: Edit the 1.8.2 code in place to add the feature, keeping the version number so no one has to update references.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to 2.0.0 everywhere at once; semantic versioning guarantees a major release will apply cleanly.

options.label: D
options.text: Pin 2.0.0, update the renamed inputs, run lint and policy checks, apply to staging, test and monitor, then production.

grader_markdown: A major version signals breaking changes, so the team should pin the new exact version and adapt its inputs. The change should then move through the pipeline the lecture describes: automated lint and policy checks, a lower environment such as staging, tests and monitoring, and only then production. Applying to production first, assuming a major release is safe, or changing released code without a new version all remove the predictability that versioning provides.

title: Testing a module across platforms
prompt_markdown: An internal configuration module must support the company's Ubuntu and Rocky Linux servers, which start from company-prepared base images. Its only tests are unit tests that run on a laptop. Which testing plan best fits the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Add more unit tests until coverage is complete, since they are fast and need no real machines.

options.label: B
options.text: In the pipeline, run it on disposable containers or VMs from images like the company's, for each OS.

options.label: C
options.text: Test on as many operating systems and clouds as possible first, since the module may be used elsewhere.

options.label: D
options.text: Run it once by hand on a production server for each OS, and keep that server as the reference test target.

grader_markdown: Unit tests add little for infrastructure code because the behavior that breaks depends on the real target: package names, defaults, and libraries differ between distributions. Integration tests should run automatically in the pipeline on disposable containers or VMs built from images that match the organization's real baselines, one per supported platform. Testing every possible platform is costly and unnecessary for an internal module, and production servers should not serve as test targets.

title: Semantic versioning
prompt_markdown: A module follows semantic versioning (major.minor.patch). Its authors release version 1.5.0 after 1.4.2. What should consumers expect?

options.label: A
options.text: The release may remove or rename inputs, so existing callers must be updated first.

options.label: B
options.text: It adds backward-compatible functionality, so current usage should keep working.

options.label: C
options.text: It contains a bug fix alone, and no new functionality is available in this release.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a test build that usually should not be used outside the authors' own team.

grader_markdown: In semantic versioning, a minor increment signals new functionality that is backward compatible, so existing usage should keep working. Breaking changes call for a major increment, and a patch increment signals a fix that does not change the interface. The scheme sets shared expectations between module authors and consumers.

title: Explicit module versions
prompt_markdown: Why should an environment definition refer to an explicit module version rather than to "latest"?

options.label: A
options.text: So a new module release cannot change the environment until its team chooses to upgrade.

options.label: B
options.text: Because explicit versions download faster, which mainly shortens each deployment run.

options.label: C
options.text: So the module authors can patch that same version in place whenever they find a bug.

options.label: D
options.text: Because pinning makes the tool pick the newest compatible release on each run automatically.
