grader_markdown: Depending on an explicit version means the environment changes only when its owners deliberately upgrade and test the new version. Referring to "latest" puts the environment at the mercy of the module authors: any new release can change or break it. Published versions are not patched in place, and pinning does not pick newer releases.

title: Published module versions
prompt_markdown: A team published version 1.1 of a module through its release pipeline. A day later they find a bug in it. What is the appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Fix the code and overwrite the published 1.1, so consumers get the fix without a version change.

options.label: B
options.text: Delete version 1.1 from the repository, so consumers can no longer deploy anything from it.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask each consuming team to apply the fix to its own local copy of the module code.

options.label: D
options.text: Fix it in the source, test it, and publish a new version such as 1.1.1, leaving 1.1 as it is.

grader_markdown: A published version is a frozen, tested point in time that consumers rely on. Fixes go into the source, pass the release pipeline again, and appear as a new version, here a patch release. Overwriting a published version silently changes what pinned consumers deploy, and removing it or asking consumers to patch copies breaks the shared release process.

title: Value of a module
prompt_markdown: Which module design is least likely to justify the extra layer it adds?

options.label: A
options.text: A module that creates a network with its subnets, routes, and gateways from a few inputs

options.label: B
options.text: A module that applies the company's disk, tagging, and network conventions to each new VM

options.label: C
options.text: A module that wraps one resource and exposes nearly every setting of it as a parameter

options.label: D
options.text: A module that combines web servers, a database, and placement rules into one application setup

grader_markdown: A module that manages a single resource and passes nearly every setting through adds indirection without capturing any knowledge; using the resource directly is usually simpler. Modules earn their place when they combine many related resources, encode the organization's conventions, or package a repeated composition. The lecture called such a single-resource module over-designed.

title: Choosing module parameters
prompt_markdown: A team is writing an internal module that creates database servers for several application teams. Which approach to the module's parameters is most sound?

options.label: A
options.text: Expose every setting of the underlying resources, because more parameters make a module easier to use.

options.label: B
options.text: Hardcode the settings, so consumers request a module change for each difference they need.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a parameter for anything a consumer might want one day, since unused parameters usually cost nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: Expose what consumers truly vary, such as size and versions, and fix the rest; each parameter is a promise.

grader_markdown: Parameters should cover what consumers legitimately need to vary, such as size, security-relevant versions, and naming, while the rest stays fixed inside the module. Each parameter is a promise the authors must keep supporting, so unneeded parameters add logic and maintenance burden. Hardcoding everything forces a module change for every ordinary difference. Internal modules can usually expose fewer parameters than public ones because their consumers are known.

title: Open for extension
prompt_markdown: A web-server module must support a growing number of sites, each with its own host name and port. Which design applies the open-closed principle?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a new conditional block to the module code each time a team requests another site.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept a list of site definitions, so consumers add sites without changing the module.

options.label: C
options.text: Copy the module for each new site and adjust the copy, so the sites can stay independent.

options.label: D
options.text: Support one site in the module, and let teams edit server files by hand for extra sites.

grader_markdown: The open-closed principle keeps a module open for extension and closed for modification. A list of site definitions is an extension point: consumers add sites by changing their inputs, and the module code stays the same. Adding conditionals or copying the module changes or duplicates its code for each request, and manual edits bypass the module.

title: Module contracts
prompt_markdown: A module installs and configures a MySQL database. A team asks for it to install PostgreSQL as well, selected by a parameter. What is the strongest design response?

options.label: A
options.text: Build a separate module; the engines differ, and one interface would fill with engine-specific inputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the parameter, because a module with more options can usually serve more consumers at little extra cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the parameter, since an engine choice is a simple pass-through value, much like an instance size.

options.label: D
options.text: Refuse the request, because a module must never gain new options once its first version is published.

grader_markdown: MySQL and PostgreSQL need different configuration, so supporting both behind one parameter roughly doubles the module's logic and fills its interface with inputs that apply to only one engine. That is a different contract and is better served by a separate module. An instance size is a simple pass-through value; an engine choice is not. Modules can gain options in new versions, so refusing all change is not the principle.

title: Patching through parameters
prompt_markdown: A vulnerability is announced in the database package version used in every environment. The module that installs the package takes its version as a parameter. What is the most suitable response?

options.label: A
options.text: Wait for a new module release, because a package version change requires new module code.

options.label: B
options.text: Edit the module code in each environment's copy, so production can be patched before the others.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the version value in the environment configurations and roll it out; no module release is needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Hardcode the fixed version inside the module, so environments can no longer choose different versions.

grader_markdown: When a patchable package version is a module parameter, patching becomes a configuration change in each environment, rolled out through the usual process; the module code and its release stay unchanged. The environments share the module's structure while their parameter values differ. A new module release is needed only when the fix changes the module's structure or logic, such as a major package upgrade.

title: Shared module across teams
prompt_markdown: A platform team owns a network module used by teams B, C, and D. Team B urgently needs a new optional feature, team C is still on an older version, and the platform team worries about breaking anyone. Which arrangement best balances speed and safety?

options.label: A
options.text: Let team B contribute it under agreed tests and policy checks, release a new minor version, announce it, and let teams upgrade when ready.

options.label: B
options.text: Let team B edit the module and republish the current version number, so consumers get the feature at once without editing their own definitions.

options.label: C
options.text: Have team B fork the module into its own repository and maintain it there, since separate copies usually avoid coordination between the teams.

options.label: D
options.text: Freeze the module until the teams agree on one roadmap, then require every consumer to upgrade to each new release on the day it is published.

grader_markdown: With shared ownership and agreed guardrails (tests, static and policy checks, and test infrastructure), any team can contribute a change safely. Releasing it as a new backward-compatible version and announcing it lets team B adopt it at once while teams C and D upgrade on their own schedule. Republishing an existing version breaks the isolation that pinned versions provide, forks let the copies diverge, and forced upgrades remove the consumers' control.

title: Reusing and writing modules
prompt_markdown: An organization runs VMs on an on-premises virtualization platform and networks and databases in a public cloud. It is starting to codify this infrastructure and has several company conventions for VMs. Which plan uses modules best?

options.label: A
options.text: Write internal modules for every component, including the cloud networks, so the company controls the code and depends on no external releases.

options.label: B
options.text: Use public registry modules throughout, and apply company conventions such as tagging and disk sizing by hand, since they usually change too often.

options.label: C
options.text: Use well-maintained public modules at pinned versions for generic parts, and write internal modules for company concepts such as a standard VM.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep everything in one project without modules until the cloud and on-premises parts use identical tools, and then start splitting it up.

grader_markdown: Start by checking the available providers and existing modules: a well-maintained public module for a generic component, such as a cloud network, saves effort and testing and can be used at a pinned version. Internal modules are worth writing for concepts specific to the organization that recur, such as a standard VM with its disk, tagging, and network conventions. Rewriting generic components in-house duplicates work, manual conventions drift, and waiting for identical tools is not required to modularize.

title: GitOps and continuous delivery
prompt_markdown: How does the lecture characterize GitOps?

options.label: A
options.text: As a Kubernetes-only practice in which an agent in the cluster applies manifests from Git

options.label: B
options.text: As continuous delivery applied to infrastructure and operations code kept in Git

options.label: C
options.text: As a hosted service that stores repositories and runs their pipelines in one place

options.label: D
options.text: As a branching model in which each environment gets its own long-lived Git branch

grader_markdown: The instructor described GitOps as continuous delivery applied to a different type of code: infrastructure, configuration, and operations code kept in Git and delivered through automation. It is not limited to Kubernetes; servers, cloud resources, and other infrastructure can be managed the same way. Git hosting services provide the pipelines, but GitOps is the practice rather than the service, and the lecture did not define it as a branching model.

title: Pull-based delivery
prompt_markdown: In a pull-based GitOps setup, how do changes reach the infrastructure?

options.label: A
options.text: A pipeline in the hosted Git service connects to each target and pushes the change

options.label: B
options.text: An engineer pulls the repository to a laptop and applies the change from there

options.label: C
options.text: An agent in or near the infrastructure regularly fetches the repository and applies it

options.label: D
options.text: Each target server waits until an operator copies the new files onto it by hand

grader_markdown: In the pull model, a component running inside or near the infrastructure, such as a Puppet agent, ansible-pull, or Argo CD, periodically pulls the repository and applies the changes. Because it lives close to the infrastructure, it holds the permissions there. A pipeline that connects to the targets is the push model, and changes applied by hand or from a laptop bypass automated delivery.

title: Repository ownership
prompt_markdown: In the cross-team workflow from the lecture, who merges another team's change into the main branch of the network team's repository?

options.label: A
options.text: The team that wrote the change, as soon as its pull request passes the pipeline checks

options.label: B
options.text: The pipeline itself, which merges each pull request automatically once its checks are green

options.label: C
options.text: A central change board, which approves merges for every repository in the organization

options.label: D
options.text: The network team that owns the repository, after it reviews the checked pull request

grader_markdown: The team that owns a repository defines its structure, pipelines, and rules, and only it can push or merge to the main branch. Other teams submit pull requests; the pipeline checks them without deploying, and the owners review the green request and merge it, which triggers delivery. The pipeline informs the decision but does not replace the owners, and the lecture's aim was to avoid slow, central approval paths.

title: Continuous reconciliation
prompt_markdown: Besides declarative, versioned code and automated delivery, some definitions of GitOps add a controller that keeps reconciling the infrastructure with Git. How did the lecture treat this fourth principle?

options.label: A
options.text: As essential, because GitOps without a controller inside a Kubernetes cluster is not GitOps

options.label: B
options.text: As optional, because scheduled pipeline runs can do much of the same checking against Git

options.label: C
options.text: As harmful, because a controller that keeps changing the infrastructure itself causes drift

options.label: D
options.text: As a replacement for version control, because the controller stores the desired state itself

grader_markdown: The lecture listed four GitOps principles: declarative code, versioned and immutable code, automatic delivery, and a desired state controller that keeps checking the target against the code. The instructor called the fourth principle optional: GitOps works without it, and scheduled pipeline runs can provide much of the same continuous verification. GitOps is not limited to Kubernetes, and such a controller works from the code in Git rather than replacing version control.

title: Push-based delivery
prompt_markdown: A team's pipelines run in a public hosted CI/CD service. They run the provisioning and configuration tools that push changes into the company's private infrastructure. What does this push model require the team to consider?

options.label: A
options.text: The CI/CD service needs network access and credentials for the targets, which must be secured.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing beyond a pull model, because both models need the same access to the infrastructure.

options.label: C
options.text: Pull requests stop working, because a push model delivers direct commits to the main branch instead.

options.label: D
options.text: Changes can no longer be traced, because a pushed change leaves no record in the repository.

grader_markdown: In the push model, the CI/CD service runs tools such as Terraform, Ansible, or Helm and connects directly to the infrastructure, so it needs network access and credentials for the targets. When the CI/CD service is public rather than internal, that access must be secured carefully. Pull requests and commit history work the same way in both models, and the lecture considered either model workable depending on the tools and security requirements.

title: Pipelines as guardrails
prompt_markdown: Why does the lecture call a repository's CI/CD pipeline guardrails for the team that owns the repository?

options.label: A
options.text: It deploys each pull request to production at once, so users find mistakes quickly.

options.label: B
options.text: It replaces human review, so owners no longer look at changes that other teams propose.

options.label: C
options.text: Its checks block changes that break the owners' rules, codifying what the owners know.

options.label: D
options.text: It is maintained by a central platform team, so the owners cannot weaken its checks.

grader_markdown: The pipeline's checks, such as syntax, policy, security, and vulnerability checks, block any change that breaks the owning team's rules. The pipeline definition is code stored in the same repository and maintained by that team, so it codifies the team's knowledge. Pull request pipelines verify without deploying, and the owners still review complex or risky changes, but much of the routine review is delegated to automation.

title: Releasing and deploying applications
prompt_markdown: An application pipeline tests each build and publishes it to an artifact repository. In the GitOps setup described in the lecture, what decides which application version runs in each environment?

options.label: A
options.text: The application pipeline, which deploys each published build to every environment at once

options.label: B
options.text: Engineers, who copy artifacts to servers by hand and note the versions in a shared document

options.label: C
options.text: Each environment, which picks up the newest published artifact on its own schedule

options.label: D
options.text: The infrastructure repository, where version bumps can be committed by people or automation

grader_markdown: Application pipelines test the code and publish release artifacts to an artifact repository; the infrastructure or configuration repository then decides which version runs in which environment. Version bumps can be committed automatically by other pipelines, so the repository has both human and automated authors. Releasing an artifact is thereby separated from deploying it, and each deployment remains a recorded change in Git.

title: A complete record of change
prompt_markdown: After an outage, a team must find out which change reached production, who approved it, and whether its checks passed. Some recent changes were applied from engineers' laptops. Which practice gives the team a complete record in future?

options.label: A
options.text: Deliver every change through reviewed commits and the pipeline, whose logs record each run.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask engineers to post a summary in the team chat whenever they apply a change from a laptop.

options.label: C
options.text: Take a snapshot of production every night, and compare snapshots when an incident happens.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the pipeline for routine work, but let senior engineers apply urgent changes directly.

grader_markdown: The commit history shows who changed what and why, the pull request shows the review, and the pipeline logs show when each change ran and with what result; observability then shows the state of the infrastructure. The record is complete only when automation is the single path for changes. Changes applied from laptops or directly by senior engineers bypass it, and chat messages or snapshots do not show who approved a change or whether its checks passed.

title: Replacing tickets with pull requests
prompt_markdown: A database team often needs small network changes, such as an opened port or a new route, in the network team's infrastructure repository. Each request goes through tickets and takes days of back-and-forth for a change of a few lines. Both teams are technical. Which workflow best fits the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the database team administrator access to the network devices, so it can make small changes itself and inform the network team afterwards.

options.label: B
options.text: Let the database team push to the main branch of the network repository, so its changes deploy at once and the network team reviews them later.

options.label: C
options.text: Let the database team open pull requests whose pipeline checks run without deploying; the network team reviews green ones and merging deploys them.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the tickets, but have the network team collect them for a weekly maintenance window, so that the requested changes are reviewed together.

grader_markdown: Pull requests to the owning team's repository replace the ticket back-and-forth that the lecture called "cosmic ping pong". The owners' pipeline checks each request automatically and gives feedback without deploying; the owners review a green request when they can and merge it, and the merge delivers the change. The owners keep control of the main branch while delegating implementation to the requesting team and much of the review to automation. Direct device access or direct pushes remove that control, and batching tickets keeps the delays.

title: Layer repositories and simple interfaces
prompt_markdown: An organization keeps its infrastructure in one repository per layer (network, machine images, server configuration, and application deployment), each owned by one team. Other teams often need to add simple entries, such as DNS records or batch jobs, to layers they do not own, while the owners keep refactoring the internals. Which organization best supports both kinds of change?

options.label: A
options.text: Merge the layers into one repository that every team can change directly, so no team waits for an owner to act.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the internals with the owners, and expose simple data files that others change through checked pull requests.

options.label: C
options.text: Let each team copy the layers it needs into its own repository and apply its copy independently of the owners.

options.label: D
options.text: Freeze the internals and route outside requests through tickets, so that the owners make every change themselves.

grader_markdown: The owning team stays responsible for the complex internals of its layer, but changes that other teams need often should be easy to make: simple interface files such as YAML or JSON in the repository, sometimes a separate repository or a self-service portal, changed through pull requests that the owners' pipeline checks. In the lecture's example, batch jobs moved into a repository that the data warehouse team could change under policy and security checks, which ended the waiting. A shared repository without owners, private copies, and tickets for every change each lose either control or flow.
